Near the end of his life, this man was said to have climbed Mount Kun Lun. He was told to write (*) five thousand characters after Yinxi stopped him at the Hangu pass. From those characters, he produced a work that includes the directive "He who knows does not speak" among its eighty-one chapters, popularizing the concept of wu-wei. For 10 points, name this mythical author of the Tao Te Ching.

The sum of the squares of the reciprocals of this function evaluated at the nonnegative integers is equal to the modified Bessel function of the first kind at x=2. The Leviathan Number is found by evaluating this function at 10 to the 666th power. The rising type can be represented with the Pochhammer Symbol. Wilson's Theorem states that this function of any prime minus 1 is also congruent to -1 modulo that prime. Legendre's theorem provides a corollary to determine the number of (*) trailing zeroes of this function evaluated at nonnegative integers. When this function is evaluated at large numbers, Stirling's approximation is used. The gamma function extends this function to all complex numbers other than negative integers. For 10 points, name this function that, for positive integers n, is the product from 1 to n, and which is represented by an exclamation point.

The title character of this novel claims that a mother is "one who screams when you suffer" while being operated on by a man whose third eye bores into his soul. That character gets banned from the Men's Club for 99 years and one day, after emptying a spittoon on a laughing man. He is seduced under the pretense of a discussion of feminism by a neglected wife after being transferred by Tarp and Wrestum. Near the end of this novel, several passersby address the title character as (*) "Rinehart," a contrast to when he assaulted a tall, blond man for insulting him. Early in this novel, the title character goes to the Golden Day with Mr. Norton after partaking in a "Battle Royal" to earn the right to speak. After becoming the enemy of Dr. Bledsoe and a Caribbean man who chucks a spear at him, the title character strings 1369 light bulbs in a basement to steal electricity from a power company. For 10 points, identify this novel about a black man nobody makes an effort to recognize, written by Ralph Ellison.

One poem by this man mourns that "The rank is but the guinea's stamp" and is sometimes named for its first line "Is there for honest poverty." The narrator of one poem by this man hopes his lover receives "peace, enjoyment, love, and pleasure" and notes that "nothing could resist my Nancy" after asking for a kiss before they "sever." One character created by this man ignores the advice of his wife Kate and nicknames the witch (*) Nannie "Cutty-sark" after wandering home from a pub. The narrator of another of his poems promises "And I will come again my love, Tho' it were ten thousand mile" after declaring "my love is like a red, red rose." For 10 points, name this author of "A Fond Kiss" and "Tam o' Shanter," a Scottish poet known for his use of dialect.

This man introduced a bill attempting to use the extra proceeds from the Second Bank of the United States to construct a national highway, which was vetoed by Madison and called the Bonus Bill. He created the Bureau of Indian affairs without congressional approval as Secretary of War during the Era of Good Feelings. His wife Floride provoked the (*) Petticoat affair by ostracizing Peggy Eaton. This man was elected vice-president in 1824 despite attacking the Corrupt Bargain, and he would be elected vice-president again four years later as part of Andrew Jackson's ticket. He opposed the Tariff of Abominations by writing the South Carolina Exposition and Protest, which positioned him as a leading advocate of nullification. For 10 points, name this influential South Carolina politician.

One application of this equation is used in speedometers of planes, called pitot-static [pih-toh] tubes. One law that can be derived from this equation states that the velocity is equal to the square root of twice the product of gravity and height, called Torricelli's law. It can be used to derive why the pressure drops in a constricted section of a pipe, called the (*) Venturi effect. This equation and Newton's laws of motion can be used to explain aerodynamic forces like lift on an airplane. A consequence of this equation is that when the velocity of a liquid is faster, the pressure is lower. For 10 points, name this equation named for a Dutch-Swiss mathematician.

One of this brand's commercials features Bruce Campbell playing "Hungry Like the Wolf" on the piano, and another ends with Neil Patrick Harris jamming a stethoscope into a patient's face. Another spokesman from this brand catches a cake while walking on water and jumps into a motorcycle inside a hot tub in one commercial. In another of their commercials, Isaiah Mustafa finds "two tickets to that thing you love" in an oyster before abruptly declaring (*) "I'm on a horse." That spokesman also declared his love for Alyssa Milano and replied to almost 200 tweets and celebrities while wearing a towel in a series of YouTube videos recorded in a bathroom over two days. For 10 points, name this hygiene brand represented by a logo of a white boat on a red background.

This artist painted a woman in blue and white striped stockings whose dress slips off her left shoulder as she dozes off on a red chair in his Sleeping Girl with a Cat. He painted a young girl wearing a flowery hat and standing next to her mother in front of a metal rail in On the Terrace. A man gazes through binoculars in his La Loge, and he painted two young sisters in elaborate lace dresses in a work often called (*) Pink and Blue. He painted hundreds of people dancing and eating under the acacia trees and lights of a Parisian locale in one work. The action of another of his paintings occurs under a red canopy, where Gustave Caillebotte and other notaries eat along the Seine. For 10 points, name this French impressionist of Le moulin de la Galette and The Luncheon of the Boating Party.

One deity in this mythological system is sometimes depicted as a dancing skeleton smoking a cigarette. That god, Cizin is also known for wearing a collar with nerves and eyes hanging from it. According to this mythology, a set of four brothers known as the Bacab hold up the sky from each of the four cardinal positions. A prominent place in this belief system is guarded by (*) three rivers of blood, pus, and scorpions, and those who enter it are often tricked into sitting on a hot surface to entertain the rulers One Death and Seven Death along with their companions. The story of that underworld, Xibalaba, is chronicled in the Popol Vuh. For 10 points, name this Mesoamerican mythology which features a pair of Hero Twins.

One ruler of this name wrote the epic poem Kingis Quair, while a later ruler of this name had a large artillery superiority in shooting down Branxton Hill. Another man with this name maintained his position as the leader of the Royal Navy despite his failure to defend against the Raid of the Medway. One monarch of this name died at Flodden Field, and another ended the (*) Monmouth Rebellion. The penultimate ruler of this name married Anne of Denmark, while the last ruler of this name fell after the Glorious Revolution. The penultimate ruler of this name had his men remove explosives placed under Parliament before it was too late. For 10 points, name this common name whose most famous member was the first monarch to unify England and Scotland, was the target of the Gunpowder Plot, and created a namesake Bible.

One class in this phylum expels their sticky cuvierian tubules through evisceration to confuse predators. Many classes in this phylum have a calcerous duct called a stone canal, which extends from an external porous calcareous plate which takes in water from outside the body. That plate is called the madreporite, which is where sea water enters the (*) water vascular system of this phylum. An important feature of this phylum is its many small tubular projections that allow locomotion and feeding, called tube feet. This phylum begins as a bilaterally symmetric free-swimming larvae, and differs from other triptoblastic animals by undergoing metamorphosis and becoming radial symmetric. Behind Chordata, this phylum is the largest group of deteurostomes, and contains the classes Asteroidea and Holothuroidea. For 10 points, name this phylum, which contains animals such as sea cucumbers and sea stars, and whose name is Greek for "spiny skin".

Both the reverse-delete algorithm and its inverse, Kruskal's algorithm, can be used to find one of these objects with the cut property, whose edges have a minimum total weight. These structures are undirected graphs which are also connected and acyclic. One of these structures invented by Adelson-Velskii and Landis is self-balancing, and is closely related to another type defined by alternating nodes of two (*) namesake colors, red and black. Heaps are considered a specialized binary type of this object, and internal connection points within them are known as forks. For 10 points, identify this type of data structure in which each node has one or fewer parents but many children, which may be rooted or planted.

This man's namesake rule allows candidates to simultaneously run for the senate and the vice presidency. He won a Senate seat election with the help of a rented helicopter nicknamed the "City Windmill." He quoted the lyrics to "America the Beautiful" in his "Let Us Continue" speech. His use of the so-called "Treatment" to strong arm dissident party members was discussed in the biography (*) Master of the Senate by Robert Caro. As president, he worked with the 89th congress to pass the Freedom of Information and Higher Education Acts, and gave the "We Shall Overcome" speech in response to the violence in Selma. This president signed the Voting Rights Act and the Social Security Act as part of his Great Society. For 10 points, name this successor to John F. Kennedy.

One commander at this battle said that all his battalions charged at least four times during the battle. The prelude to this battle consisted of crafty maneuvering down the Rhine by the British, away from the Dutch and toward the forces of Marshal Tallard and the Elector of Bavaria. The major mistake of the losing side was the excessive requisitioning of troops into the namesake city. (*) Eugene of Savoy commanded one wing of the Allies and John Churchill commanded the wing. For ten points, name this battle, that saved Vienna from being taken by the Franco-Bavarian army, the turning point of the War of Spanish Succession.

In the right edge of this painting, a figure's eye bulges as he appears to be dragged down by his genitals. A disembodied orange head poking out from the thigh of a figure holding a gold key is possibly the artist's self-portrait. A group of figures holds a large Doric column in the air in the upper right of this painting. One figure in the lower center holds open a white book just to the right of two men dangling on a tether of rope. A fiery creature crouches under a green rock arch besides people who are changing into skeletons. Another creature is about to whack a group of people on a boat with an oar while directing them towards the figure of snake-covered (*) Minos. Just below the central figure is St. Lawrence holding a gridiron, and to the right St. Bartholomew holds a knife in his right hand and his own flayed skin in his left. The title action of this painting involves a bent-elbowed figured with a yellow background behind him who bears the marks of the stigmata. For 10 points, identify this Michelangelo painting on the wall of the Sistine Chapel, depicting the end of the world.

Much to the chagrin of its librettist Friedrich Kind, this opera's original opening scene, in which a hermit has a terrible vision of the future, was cut from the final version. A diminished seventh chord accompanies seven manifestations of evil in a scene taking place in the Wolf's Glen, and in this opera's first act the drinking song "Hier im ird'schen Jammerthal" is sung in order to enrage the protagonist, who wants to marry the daughter of Cuno. In Act II, Aennchen accidentally knocks down (*) a portrait, hurting a woman who dreams that she will be killed in the form of a white dove; that woman also makes a bridal wreath using a possibly-magical rose and is named Agathe. After he is defeated in a contest by the peasant Killian, the protagonist Max is shown by the forester Caspar the power of magic bullets that will allow him to win the marksman's competition the next day. For 10 points, name this opera by Carl Maria von Weber.
Der Freischütz [accept The Free-Shooter or The Marksman before that word is read]

He painted a woman in a white cap who holds an animal munching on an acorn in his Portrait of a Lady with a Squirrel and a Starling. Many of this artist's early works were commissioned by Jakob Meyer, who is seen with his family in The Darmstadt Madonna. Dostoyevsky was obsessed with this man's realistically grotesque The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb. He painted the Greek for "the Labors of Hercules on a red book held by (*) Erasmus, on whose recommendation he was commissioned to paint Thomas More. In a lost work, he painted a king holding a glove in one hand and a dagger in the other. He included a wildly skewed skull in his portrait of Jean de Dinteville and Georges de Selve. For 10 points, name this court painter to Henry VIII who painted The Ambassadors.

An account of this thinker's later life was given in Beatrice Potter's My Apprenticeship, while he himself encouraged writers to break away from conventional prose in "Philosophy of Style." One of his essays argues that governments' actions should be limited to upholding and protecting natural rights, while another of his works posits that the "multiplication of effects" follows from the "law of persistence force." In addition to The Proper Sphere of Government and First Principles, he also wrote about "New Toryism" and the limiting of powers of both Parliament and the monarchy in (*) Man Versus the State. Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. referenced one of this man's works in his dissenting opinion in Lochner v. New York, and this author of System of Synthetic Philosophy is also known for his Lamarckian view of evolution. For 10 points, name this British thinker, the author of Social Statics and the coiner of the phrase "survival of the fittest."

One act signed by this president was named after a man who was tortured and murdered in Wyoming and another after a man who was decapitated in Texas and provided fifteen million dollars to local authorities over a three year time span to fight a certain type of criminal offense. Another act signed by this president amended the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to alter the definition of a 180 day time-stamp that had caused a woman suing (*) Goodyear company to have her case struck down in the Supreme Court. The Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act and the Lily Ledbetter Fair Pay Act were both passed under the tenure of this president, who reversed his predecessor's policy of cutting funding to foreign organizations that allowed abortion. For 10 points, name this person who was succeeded as a Senator by Roland Burris.

Ba'al is sometimes depicted as one of these animals. One of these creatures worshipped in Memphis was originally called the Herald of Ptah, and was later identified as a god of the dead, Apis. In Hindu myth, one which emerged during the churning of the ocean was named Surabhi. One appearing briefly in the Prose Edda is (*) Audhumla. The steed of Shiva is one of these animals named Nandi, and Gilgamesh and Enkidu killed one "of heaven." As an infant, Hermes stole some of these belonging to Apollo, while others belonging to Geryon were stolen by Heracles. This animal is used to depict the Egyptian goddess of love and fertility, Hathor. Pasiphae mated with this type of creature which, for 10 points, forms the head of the resulting offspring, the Minotaur.

Fluoroacetate is a potent toxin because one of its metabolites blocks an important enzyme in this pathway. One of its intermediates is a precursor for both aminolevulinate and eventually porphyrins. The molecules consumed in this pathway are replenished by anaplerotic reactions. This process results in the reduction of one molecule of ubiquinone via an (*) FADH2 intermediary, and its only membrane-bound step is the conversion of succinate to fumarate. This process occurs within the mitochondrial matrix, and is followed by oxidative phosphorylation. For 10 points, name this pathway which contributes to the electron transport chain, an aerobic process central to cellular respiration.
Krebs cycle [or tricarboxylic acid cycle or citric acid cycle]

One poem by this author describes a wall inscribed with the phrase "PARAS THIRTEEN, BOGSIDE NIL" and is an elegy for a man who "drank like a fish" before he was "blown to bits." He included the image of a "four foot box, a foot for every year" in a poem narrated by a student who "sat all morning in the college sick bay counting bells knelling classes to a close." This author of "Casualty" wrote of a student of Miss Walls who collects "jampotfulls" of (*) "frogspawn" in another poem. He wrote that "my squat pen rests" "between my finger and my thumb" in a poem that compares his profession to his father's labor in the bogs. For 10 points, name this poet who included "Mid-Term Break" and "Digging" in his collection The Death of a Naturalist, an Irish Nobel winner who translated Beowulf.

In one story by this author, Princess Amasidia is sentenced to death for shouting the name of her exiled lover after Mambres learns he is trapped in the body of the title animal. In another of his works, Giroflee becomes a carpenter after falling in love with Paquette and moving to the title character's farm. This author of "The White Bull" wrote a story about a friend of Cador who cuckolds the Babylonian king Moabdar when he falls in love with (*) Astarte. Another of this author's protagonist befriends the Manichee Martin and the Anabaptist Jacques, who drowns during the Lisbon earthquake. The protagonist of that work is kicked out of Baron Thunder-Ten-Tronckh's castle because of his love for Cunegonde. For 10 points, name this French author of Zadig who included the optimistic Pangloss in Candide.

The title event of one of this man's poems happens as "Teeny was about to cough" and "Ralph the Lion was engaged in biting the neck of Madame Sossman." In another work, this poet wrote about the "always coming on / the always rising of the night." He wrote of the "nothing, nothing, nothing - nothing at all" occurring in a sonnet which opens "Quite unexpectedly" and is titled "The End of the World." This poet used the image of (*) "An empty doorway and a maple leaf" in one of his poems, and the narrator of another sits "face down beneath the sun" and reflects on Ecbatan, Baghdad, and Palmyra. This author of "You, Andrew Marvell" wrote that "a poem should be palpable and mute as a globed fruit" in his "Ars Poetica." For 10 points, name this author of the verse drama J.B.

In Islam, a prayer called the Salat al-Janazah is spoken before and on behalf of these entities. Jewish advocacy groups and the Vatican have vehemently attacked the Mormon practice, promoted by James Strang, of baptizing them. Because they are not allowed to contaminate the earth or fire in (*) Zoroastrianism, they are given to the birds in Dakhmas or "Towers of Silence." In their honor, adherents of Judaism wear a torn garment called the keriah during the seven days of sitting shiva. Most indulgences were purchased to benefit them and the Kaddish is often said for them in Judaism. For 10 points, name these entities that either go to heaven or hell in Christianity.

This man has a daughter named Random Frequent Flyer. He is called a "complete kneebiter" by Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged, and the Bird People of Brontitall live in the ear of a giant statue of this man. While living on Lamuella, he holds the title of "Official Sandwich Maker" for his village. He once attempted to teach cavemen how to play Scrabble, and later taught a girl named (*) Fenchurch to fly. This man is shot in a club owned by Stavro Mueller, and his brain is coveted by characters named Benjy and Frankie. Soon after we first meet this character, his home is destroyed by Mr. L. Prosser. For 10 points, name this character perpetually in search of a cup of tea, who "never could get the hang of Thursdays," the protagonist of the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.

The void type of this in C can be used to store any data type. Wild and dangling ones can lead to segmentation faults. In linked lists, it is used to connect to the next element and a null type of this is used at the end of the linked list. It is used to(*) dynamically allocate memory and if the memory is not deallocated, a memory leak will occur. In C and C++, arrays can be dereferenced using this construct rather than using brackets. In the C and C++ programming languages, it is defined using an asterisk. For 10 points, name this construct in computer science that refers to an address of another value.

Overconsumption of this nutrient has been linked to long-term decreases in bone density and increased intracranial pressure. All forms of this nutrient contain an identical structural motif, a beta-ionone attached to an isoprenoid chain. This nutrient has a carboxylic acid metabolite that maintains (*) skin integrity and acts to transcribe certain genes. This nutrient's most famous function, however, is mediated by another form, which binds to opsin and isomerizes upon stimulation by light. For ten points, name this essential fat-soluble nutrient, plentiful in both the liver and carrots, whose deficiency causes night blindness.

Many of this policy's goals were drawn from the research of Seebohm Rowntree, who isn't Henry George, but published a study named Progress and Poverty. The economist Arthur Seldon argued heavily against this policy, whose name was coined by William Temple. Asa Briggs outlined three of its main goals in a 1967 article, and Richard Titmuss wrote a series of essays about it. Gunnar Myrdal analyzed "Economic planning and its international implications" in a book titled for going beyond this policy. It was outlined in a paper that delineated five (*) "great evils" in society, which were squalor, ignorance, want, idleness, and disease. Including the Butler Act and the formation of the National Health Service, it arose during the tenure of Prime Minister Clement Attlee. For 10 points, give the term for these socialist policies implemented in the wake of the Beveridge Report.

The Tassili-N-Ajjer is a long northwest-trending ridge located just west of the Haggar Mountains while the El Djouf is border on the east by the Tagant Plateau, which holds several gueltas that harbor resident crocodile populations. The Tanezrouft Basin in is located in this area Bualus Period names the earliest known rock art in this region, such as that at Gilf Kebir which contains the "Cave of the Swimmers," and this region is theorized to have acted as a period "Pump" during the Neolithic Subpluvial. A major scheme to pump water from the Sirt and Kufra basins in this area is actively underway and a major music festival in this region is held at (*) Essouk. The first French nuclear tests took place in this area which includes the Grand Ergs as well as the Great Sand Sea. For 10 points, identify this desert north of the Sahel.

This substance binds to synaptotagmin to stimulate the SNARE-mediated fusion of synaptic vesicles to the cell membrane. Along with heat, bacterial cells are treated with its chloride to make them competent, allowing the uptake of free plasmids. In the slow mechanism for blocking polyspermy of sea urchins, the fusion of the first sperm triggers an increase in cytoplasmic concentrations of this (*) ion that allows the vitelline layer to block subsequent sperm. It causes a conformational change in troponin C after this ion is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, opening up binding sites on myosin. For 10 points, name this ion important in muscle contraction which, which along with phosphate ions, forms hydroxyapatite, the primary mineral in bone.

This polity and Uruguay won the Battle of Caseros in the Platine War. Ernesto Geisel was a later ruler of this polity, which had a Constitution enacted in 1934. One ruler was known as the "father of the poor" for his labor legislation, while the death of Prince Imperial Afonso weakened the desire of another ruler to rule. (*) Getuilo Vargas was a later ruler of this country, which later saw the Positivists gain power after Isabel proclaimed the unpopular abolition of slavery in the Golden Law. This polity gained independence following Napoleon's invasion of Portugal, and its royal house was of the House of Braganza. For 10 points, name this polity once ruled by Pedro II with cities like Sao Paulo.

One character in this play complains about the "marsh vapors" in his room and leaves a large puddle while trying to extinguish a fire. Another room in this play is filled with pictures of exotic lands procured by its former tenant, an old sea captain nicknamed "The Flying Dutchman." A dinner part in its first act sparks the recurring theme of thirteen men at the table. Molvik is convinced that he is possessed by demons by (*) Dr. Relling, a man whose doctrine of illusion clashes with Greger's insistence on truth. The photographer Hialmar constantly seeks a great invention in this play in an effort to provide for the ailing daughter he suspects may have been fathered by Hakon Werle. For 10 points, name this Henrik Ibsen play which ends with Hedvig Ekdal shooting herself instead of the title bird.

One of this author's novellas centers on a girl who is shocked by Miss Stanley's uneducated nature while she is living under the care of her aunt Mrs. Percival; that protagonist misses her sisters, who are sent to India and Scotland. Another novella by this author contains an amusing scene in which the Lord St. Clair gives out four fifty pound notes to a succession of strangers who he serendipitously believes to be his grandchildren; in that work, Augustus, the husband of Sophia, is sent to debtor's prison, as is related by the narrator, Laura. In addition to Catherine, or, the Bower, and (*) Love and Friendship, she wrote a novel whose title character is attracted to Frank Churchill but ends up marrying Mr. Knightley. For 10 points, name this author of Emma and Pride and Prejudice.

The majority opinion in this case notes that California's continual invocation of worthless remedies is "buttressed by the experience of other States." The dissent alludes to "untoward practical ramifications" that would be had regarding the in forma pauperis cases that relied on the legal procedure invalidated by this case. The dissent also mentions that an inability to recognize the weight carried by stare decisis made it seem like the Court "reached out" to overturn (*) Wolf v. Colorado. This case saw Justice Clark note that "Nothing can destroy a government more quickly than its failure to observe its own laws." The Boyd and Weeks decisions provided precedents for this case, which exemplified the "fruit of the poisonous tree" doctrine with regards to a trunk of pornographic materials. For 10 points, identify this case which ruled that the exclusionary rule made evidence taken by the Cleveland police inadmissible in court.

This god once helped out Hera after she promised him one of the Graces, Pasithia, as his wife, and he shares with his brother the symbol of an inverted torch. One of his sons is also known by the name Icelus, and in book sixteen of the Iliad he carries the body of Sarpedon back to Lycia with his brother, whose Roman equivalent is Mors. He lives either on the island of Lemnos (*) or in a cave through which the river Lethe flows, and this deity is the son of Erebus and Nyx, both of whom are associated with darkness. Often depicted with wings attached to his head, this god is also the brother of Thanatos and the father of the Oneiroi, a group of beings which include Phobetor, Phantasos, and Morpheus; that group brings him the dreams of mortals. For 10 points, name this Greek god of sleep.

Several members of this state's powerful Railroad Commission have already announced for the 2012 Senate election. The current governor of this state announced that he supports House Concurrent Resolution 50. One governing body in this state, led by dentist Don McLeroy, passed language to change references to the United States government to a "constitutional republic," rather than "democratic," and "imperialism" to "expansionism." Debra Medina was a Tea Party candidate in this state's 2010 Republican gubernatorial primary, which saw a rare clash between a sitting (*) governor and sitting US Senator. Current Democratic gubernatorial candidate Bill White was formerly mayor of this state's largest city, which is currently led by Annise Parker, its first openly gay mayor. Politicians intervened to help keep the Big 12 together in, for 10 points, what US State where Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison is retiring and Governor Rick Perry has spoken fondly of secession?

Its namesake edge is formed in gamma ray spectroscopy when a gamma ray scatters off the detector because of this effect. The Klein-Nishima formula gives the generalized formula for both this and the Thomson effect for all frequencies. The inverse of this effect can be observed when photons in the cosmic microwave background interact with hot gas near a galaxy group, known as the (*) Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect. The change in wavelength from this effect is equal to Planck's constant divided by the mass of an electron and the speed of light multiplied by one minus the cosine of the scattering angle. For 10 points, name this effect in which a high frequency photon loses energy when it interacts with matter, and inelastic effect named for an American scientist.

This city is the proposed location of Rem Koolhas's death star shaped convention center, a feature of his master plan for a Waterfront City here. Its Jumeira Beach is the location of the Hydropolis Underwater Hotel, and the glossy sheen of its 21st Century Tower is often blanketed with a giant advertisement. This city contains the world's tallest hotel in the Rose Tower, and one of its towers was built to resemble a (*) dhow's sail and has a heli-pad which hosted a tennis match between Andre Agassi and Roger Federer. This city is also home to artificial lagoons called The Palm Islands and the World Islands, and its mainland attractions include the Burj al-Arab and the Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world. For 10 points, name this largest of the United Arab Emirates.

A study of the planet HD209548b involved the use of this equation to model the planet's clouds. The model predicted by this equation changes slightly between particles having an attractive Yukawa potential. This equation can model the equilibrium between (*) water vapor and a hydrated compound. It is derived from a similarly named equation that relates pressure to temperature, volume, and latent heat. In essence, solving this equation will yield the coexistence curve for two states of a substance. Its simplest form states that delta P over delta T equals L over T delta V. For 10 points, name this doubly eponymous equation, which demonstrates a nonlinear relationship between the temperature and vapor pressure of a system.

The titular animals of one of this author's poems "sat of a fence rail, / Thinking of effect and cause, / Of weeds and flowers, / And nature's laws." The title creature of another of his poems "lived in a box" and "swam in a puddle" and, though "he caught the flea," "he didn't catch me." In addition to "Two Old Crows" and "The Little Turtle," he wrote about a figure whose heart is broken because "kings must murder still." This author of (*) "Abraham Lincoln Walks at Midnight" also wrote a poem about a geographical feature that is "creeping through the black" and "Cutting through the forest with a golden track." His best known poem is about a figure whose "Eyes still dazzled by the ways of God;" that poem repeatedly asks "Are you washed in the blood of the lamb?" For 10 points, name this author of "The Congo" and "General William Booth Enters Into Heaven."

This author described "mildew of summer and the deepening snow" in a poem ending "one might in turn become less diffident." He wrote of "her desire for June and evening, tipped/by the consummation of the swallow's wings" in one poem, and described green, yellow, and blue rings on purple, green, and yellow nightgowns in another. This author described "Coffee and oranges in a sunny chair" as the (*) "complacencies of the peignoir," and wrote of "icicles fill[ing] the long window/with barbaric glass" and "let be be finale of seem." In those two poems, he mentioned the "golden birds" not imagined by the "thin men of Haddam," and the "concupiscent curds" whipped by "the roller of big cigars." For 10 points, identify this American poet of "Sunday Morning," "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," and "The Emperor of Ice-Cream."

This country gained the Protectorate of Wituland in the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty. A perceived treaty violation by king Ovonramwen and the cessation of palm oil trading led forces from this country to destroy the Kingdom of Benin. One of its colonies was depicted on the Zuniga Map and is the subject of a theory known as the "Lumbee Connection." This country's colony at Surat was founded after it won the battle of Swally, but was only profitable until this country acquired (*) Bombay as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry. This country administered its colonies of Malacca, Penang, and Labuan under the Straights Settlement, which also encompassed Singapore. For 10 points, name this country which won Gibraltar from Spain at Utrecht and established colonies at Roanoke and Jamestown.

In one scene from this film, a student continually spills ink on his notebook and tears the pages out until he runs out. In another scene, that character pulls his black turtleneck up to his eyes. That protagonist attends a puppet show version of Little Red Riding Hood, during which the camera focuses on the faces of dozens of little children. The central character of this film visits a carnival and rides a spinning machine called the Rotor. After joining his friend Rene in (*) stealing a typewriter from his father, the protagonist of this film is sent to a detention camp by the sea. Its conclusion depicts its protagonist escaping from a soccer game and running into the surf. For 10 points, name this film about the juvenile delinquent Antoine Doinel, directed by Francois Truffaut.

This disorder would fall on the opposite end of a spectrum from autism in a recent model proposed by Simon Baron Cohen, and Harry Stack Sullivan wrote a text titled for it as Human Process. Newer treatments for this condition, like clozapine, target serotonin receptors, and are replacing older drugs like haloperidol, which often lead to (*) tardive dyskinesia. This disorder was first termed "dementia praecox" by Emil Kraeplin, and received its current name from Eugen Bleuler. The severity of a patient's symptoms may be determined on the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale; those symptoms include waxy flexibility, flattened affect, and grandiosity. It is commonly attributed to low levels of dopamine. For 10 points, identify this psychological disorder classed into subtypes like catatonic and paranoid.

This politician said that the Soviets "put guns before butter, while we put just about everything before guns" in the "Britain Awake" speech, which was given after rising to power during the Winter of Discontent. The term "dries" refers to supporters of the economic policies of this leader, who fell after attempting to institute a "Community Charge" tax to fund local government. The IRA attempted to assassinate this prime minister in the Brighton hotel bombings. During this PM's term, (*) Augusto Pinochet's early radar warnings helped British forces defeat General Galtieri's invasion of an island group near Tierra del Fuego. For 10 points, name this Prime Minister who fought the Falklands War and was nicknamed the "Iron Lady"

A leader of the fief of Kii who led the country during this period introduced sweet potato and sugarcane cultivation and began the compilation of the Kansei law code. Scholarly endeavors in this era were divided into the schools of Ancient Learning, National Learning, and Dutch Learning. This era included the artistic flourishing of the "original happiness period." Another ruler's attempt to stamp out Christianity during this era led to the (*) Shimabara Rebellion. During the disintegration of its namesake government, this period saw the establishment of the Ezo Republic and the Boshin War. Ended by the proclamation of the Charter Oath and rallying behind Emperor Meiji, for 10 points, identify this final Japanese shogunate which lasted from 1600 to 1858.

A technique known as ricochet is required for several of these pieces, many of which call for the extensive use of a drone note. Dedicated "to the artists," some were transcribed by Robert Schumann, who wrote accompaniments to all of them. They are not Beethoven's piano sonatas, but one is often called "The Hunt" (*) and imitates the flute on the high notes on horns on the low notes. A "detache" playing style is implemented on the thirteenth of these pieces, another of which sees double-stopped sixths followed by a series of up-bow staccatos. The nickname "The Devil's Chuckle," which adorns the thirteenth one, refers to that piece's rapid trills and its composer's apocryphal relationship with Satan. Recorded by the likes of Jascha Heifetz and Itzhak Perlman, this collection's most famous piece is its last, the subject of variations by Brahms and Rachmaninoff. For 10 points, name this group of solo violin works published by Niccolo Paganini.

Jan Gossart's depiction of this scene features a castle in the left background and an irregularly shaped central object, which can also be seen in a painting by Rosso Fiorentino. An Arabic man in pink seems to hover above the ground under the central object in the Limbourg brothers' depiction of it, while Jacopo Pontormo's Mannerist version features two young women holding a man with red hair. A woman in a dark blue dress lies on the ground while Nicodemus and (*) Joseph of Arimathea hold a man's body in a painting by Roger van der Weyden. Common elements of this scene include a large white cloth and ladders, which people use to reach and secure the central figure, who is usually covered in blood. Peter Paul Rubens created several versions of, for 10 points, what common scene which depicts a certain religious figure being taken down shortly after his death by crucifixion?
The Descent from the Cross or The Deposition of Christ

The genes coding for these molecules are purposefully mutated in a process called somatic hypermutation, and they sometimes undergo isotype switching. In a process discovered by Susumu Tonegawa, they are assembled by random selection of variable region, diversity, and joining segments, called V(D)J recombination. Both the nonspecific and specific type of these molecules are used in (*) ELISA. They enhance phagocytosis in a process called opsonization, and activate the binding of proteins C1 through C9 in the complement cascade. They fall into five major classes: G, A, M, D, and E. For 10 points, identify these bivalent Y-shaped proteins consisting of two light and two heavy chains, which recognize the epitopes of specific pathogens.

Yale's M. Keith Hall claimed the Monty Hall Effect nullified the results of an experiment in which these animals were given various colored M&M's to prove they suffer from cognitive dissonance. In a thought experiment, these animals are conditioned to attack the more ambitious members of their group with blasts of cold water. Joseph Brady shocked an "Executive" one every time it failed to press a lever, until it died of stress induced ulcers. One experiment on these animals was described in (*) "The Nature of Love" and involved constructing one from wire and another from terrycloth. In another experiment, they were placed in a chamber nicknamed the "pit of despair." For 10 points, Harry Harlow experimented on the Rhesus variety of what primate?

This thinker used the last name Oswald to publish a series of articles which earned him a place in The Free, a group within the Young Hegelians, whom he later criticized along with Bruno Bauer in another work. The partner in romances with the sisters Elizabeth and Mary Burns, he was largely influenced by Moses Hess and argued that the titular concepts are not "natural" institutions and are obstacles to human progress in The Origin of the Family, (*) Private Property, and the State. This thinker also criticized the philosophy of another German in Anti-During, part of which was separately published as Socialism: Utopian and Scientific. Death rates before and after the introduction of mills were discussed in his The Condition of the Working Class in England. For 10 points, name this German thinker, the collaborator of Karl Marx.

This poem's line "Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky" is followed by eight stanzas of invocations to bells to "ring out" or "ring in." This poem quotes its earlier assertion that nature is "so careful of the type" but "so careless of the single life" before marveling that man "trusted God was love indeed" even though "Nature, red in tooth and claw" has "shriek'd against his creed." Its preface invokes "Strong Son of God, immortal Love," and this poem's (*) one hundred and thirty one sections are composed of ABBA quatrains sometimes known as its namesake stanza. The narrator of this poem holds that "Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all." For 10 points, name this Tennyson poem written over seventeen years after the death of Arthur Henry Hallam.

He authored a report about the relations between Britain and her dominions that proved instrumental in the phasing out of the governors-general and the implementation of High Commissioners. After the failure of the Gallipoli Campaign, he replaced Winston Churchill as First Lord of the Admiralty, and served out the rest of the war as Foreign Secretary under Lloyd George. He was nicknamed "Bloody" for his suppression of Irish dissent and during his term as PM, he entered into the Entente Cordiale with France. He served as PM from (*) 1902 to 1905, and his most remembered accomplishment was actually authored by Alfred Milner. That document was addressed to Lord Rothschild and promised assistance in establishing a Jewish homeland. For 10 points, name this British politician.

One model organism of this type produces four forms of rhodopsin, including one used to create a proton gradient for ATP synthesis. Another organism of this type uses 2-oxoacid ferredoxin oxidoreductase in place of its missing alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase gene, allowing it to carry out aerobic reactions. That species is Aeropyrum pernix. One group of these organisms uses either acetate or hydrogen as a source of energy, producing a major source of marsh gas as output. Their cell membranes often contain (*) ether-linked lipids and their cell walls lack peptidoglycan. For 10 points, name this domain of organisms which includes methanogens and many extremophiles, which are more closely related to eukaryotes than bacteria.

Two characters in this novel create the Pyramid Club, an organization so exclusive that only they are part of it. One character has his car wrecked after he refuses to pay a toll enacted by some Emerald Isle firemen; his fiancee Sarah's attempt to rectify the situation results in her death at the hands of the vice president's guards. The immigrant Tateh changes his name to Baron Ashkenazy and becomes a movie tycoon in this novel, which also profiles Father's trip to the North Pole and (*) Mother's Younger Brother's revolutionary acts. The third family depicted in this novel includes the grief stricken militant Coalhouse Walker. Those families are connected by interactions with J.P. Morgan, Emma Goldman, and Harry Houdini. For 10 points, name this novel by E.L. Doctorow.

Among this deity's servants are the attendant Fulla, the guard Syn, who watches over the doors of her water-filled palace Fensalir, and the messenger Gna, who once delivered one of her apples to King Rerir. One of the two beings allowed to sit on the throne Hlidskialf, she once stole the gold from another god's statue and slept with a dwarf (*) in order to conceal the secret, prompting her husband to go into exile, during which time she may have had affairs with her brothers-in-law Vili and Ve. This fertility goddess often used a spinning wheel to create clouds. As a seer of all destinies, she was able to extract promises from all living things, except mistletoe, to not harm her son Balder. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess, the wife of Odin.

This man organized a branch of the Vatan organization during en exile in Syria. His military exploits included marching his troops through the lines of Charles Harrington with his arms reversed. He used to heights of Chunuk Bair to win one battle, in which he prevailed despite the surprise landing at Suvla Bay. His forces are sometimes blamed for the Great Fire of Smyrna started after he fought off troops sent by Eleftherios Venizelos. He eventually grew frustrated with the "Union and Progress Party," writing the Amasya Circular which called for the Sivas Congress. He mandated the use of (*) surnames, abolished the position of Caliph, and banned the fez as part of modernizations enacted after the fall of Mehmed VI. For 10 points, name this father of modern Turkey.

At the end of the novel he appears in, this character remembers that he had met his wife in Chicago, a fact he had previously forgotten. He receives a device known as "the green bullet," which allows his friend to secretly talk to him, and due to an injured leg, he is almost run over by a car driven by children, whom this character suspects of killing his neighbor. Among his coworkers are the quiet Black and Stoneman, while other characters he encounters include his wife's friends (*) Mrs. Phelps and Mrs. Bowles, to whom he reads "Dover Beach." In the chapter "Burning Bright," he is told that he represents the "back-up copy" of the Book of Ecclesiastes by Granger. Earlier, he kills his boss, Captain Beatty, prompting the Mechanical Hound to hunt him down. For 10 points, name this literary character, a fireman who burns books in Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451.

One painting by this artist depicts two men grasping onto a red garment which a man on horseback cuts with his sword, while another of his works depicts a baby looking up at her father Franz Synder, a contemporary of this artist. In addition to St. Martin Dividing His Cloak and Family Portrait, he also created several pictures of St. Rosalia and the portrait George Gage, Looking at a Statuette while staying in Genoa. Other works by him include the incomplete tapestry Procession of the Knights of the Garter for the Whitehall Banqueting Hall, self-portraits "with a broken column"(*) and "with a sunflower," and the etching-collection Iconography, which may have been produced in his native Antwerp. This artist is also known for his 35 portraits of Queen Henrietta Maria, the wife of a man he famously depicted "on horseback" and "in a hunting dress." For 10 points, name this 17th century Flemish artist most famous for his many portraits of the Stuart King Charles I.

The nif regulon codes for enzymes central to this process, which may be inhibited by a shortage of alpha-ketoglutarate or excess glutamate. In some cyanobacteria, it is carried out in specialized thick-walled cells called heterocysts. Vanadium is sometimes used in an alternative co-factor to this process, but is not as common as FeMo-co, which contains homocitrate, an Fe7-S8 cube, and a (*) molybdenum center. The reductase involved in this process is irreversibly inactivated by oxygen, leading to conformational protection in free living aerobes like Azotobactor. This process is also carried out by bacteria including Rhizobium that grow in the root nodules of legumes. For 10 points, name this process which allows organisms to make use of a certain atmospheric gas by converting it to ammonia.

This thinker defined "force" as something that produces work and "progress" as "the development and economy of forces" in postulating a "dynamic theory of history." He coupled this with a theory about the exponential increase in civilization's technological proficiency he termed the "law of acceleration." One of his theories was prompted by his time wandering through the intense heat at the (*) Paris Exposition of 1900. That theory holds that attractive force of the medieval Catholic Church produces more unity than the current many faceted world of technology. This thinker probed some of these ideas in his book Mont Saint Michel and Chartres but exposed them directly in the chapter The Dynamo and the Virgin. For 10 points, name this American author of an autobiographical "education," the grandson of the second president.

In an expedition preceding the one lead by this man, the Moorish slave Black Stephen or Estevanico struck out alone ahead of the party and was allegedly killed because of his demands for women. That party was led by Fray Marcos de Niza, who stopped short when he heard of the fate of Stephen but submitted a glowing report to Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza. This man personally strangled his guide "El Turco" after his search for the city of Quivira led him only to boring tribes in (*) Kansas. After defeating some Zuni soldiers but discovering there was no treasure at Cibola, he abandoned his quest for the Seven Cities of Gold and ended up discovering the Grand Canyon and exploring the Colorado River. For 10 points, name this "last conquistador" who explored the American West.

This author discussed the "selection of bonds to be formed" and those to be neglected in the teaching of math in his work The Psychology of Arithmetic. While devising the Alpha and Beta tests for US Armed Forces to take, he postulated that age thirty-five marked the point where ability to learn diminished. This psychologist created three sets of word books with twenty to thirty thousand words each. He provided the first empirical research for an effect in which perception of one trait influences perceptions of other traits; he also attributed exercise and recency as contributing to the optimization of learning, through studies he conducted with (*) cats and puzzle boxes. For 10 points, identify this formulator of the "halo effect" and the Law of Effect, a psychologist who wrote Animal Intelligence.

During the Civil War, this state provided the Union with its Henry and Winchester rifles and Colt pistols, as well as Secretary of the Navy Gideon Welles. David Wooster died here during the Revolutionary War battle of Ridgefield, which occurred before a landing here known as Tryon's raid. Eli Whitney laid the groundwork for the industrial dominance of this state, which experienced unusual stability during the revolution because of the steady leadership of (*) Jonathan Trumbull. Its "western reserve" is now part of Ohio, and it was settled during colonial times by Thomas Hooker, who helped draft its "Fundamental Orders." During the War of 1812, this state was home to a meeting chaired by Harrison Otis which led to the demise of the Federalist Party. For 10 points, name this site of the Hartford Convention.

This event launched the career of Roger Boisjoly and resulted in an undisclosed fine for Morton Thiokol. It prompted the only ever postponement of the State of the Union speech, which was replaced by a brief address that noted the 390th anniversary of Sir Francis Drake's death. The Kerwin report noted the activation of three PEAPs during this event, and it prompted a congressional hearing which saw (*) Rogers Commission member Richard Feynman use a glass of ice water to demonstrate flaws in the O-ring. In its aftermath, Peggy Noonan wrote a speech in praise of those who "slipped the surly bonds of earth" to 'touch the face of God." For 10 points, name this event in which thousands of children witnessed the death of Christa McAuliffe, a 1987 space shuttle disaster.

One early leader of this polity failed in his attempt to modernize the hi-tech industry via the Economic System of Socialism while also failing with the New Economic System. That leader's rule also saw the creation of Intershops and the Karl-Marx Alley. Its penultimate leader created vertically integrated production systems called combines along with heavily sponsoring sports to boost prestige. Bertolt Brecht spent his final years in this polity and Egon (*) Krenz was its last leader. Its end came via Die Wende or The Change. The secret police in this country were the Stasi and its leaders have included Eric Honecker and Walter Ulbricht. For 10 points, name this polity centered at Berlin, unlike its counterpart centered at Bonn.
East Germany [accept German Democratic Republic; accept GDR; accept Deutsche Demokratische Republik; accept DDR]

The protagonist of this novel is deeply affected by his memory of watching a dung beetle while lying wounded during the Korean War. In its epilogue, the protagonist sells his duck club land to Mr. Sartalamaccia and visits Lonnie just before his death. That protagonist makes an investment in American Motors and has affairs with a series of secretaries, culminating with (*) Sharon Kincaid. Other characters in this novel include Walter Wade whose fiance attempts suicide with whiskey and sodium pentobarbital. The climax of this novel is a long moralizing lecture delivered by the protagonist's great-aunt Emily after he takes Kate Cutrer with him on a business trip before the Mardi Gras parade. For 10 points, name this novel about cinema aficionado "Binx" Bolling's search for meaning, a work of Walker Percy.

In one story, Cadmus slays one of these animals sacred to Ares and is subsequently turned into one. In another story, Hera turns Tiresias into a woman after he sees two of these animals mating and kills one of them. Typhon's wife Echidna is usually described as half-nymph and half one of these animals that kill Eurydice. One type of these animals is an enemy of (*) Apollo and is killed by him at the site of the Delphic Oracle. The Ouroboros consists of one of them biting its own tail, and two of them can be found on the Caduceus. Hera sends two of these animals in an attempt to kill a young Heracles. These animals made up the hair of the Gorgon sister Medusa. For 10 points, name these reptiles.

One character in this story might have discovered "a subtle chemistry that transmuted asses' milk to lime and phosphorus." Two foreign characters in this story are reminded of Greenwich and sing songs about the Arethusa to the title character, who is presented with wild honeysuckles and azaleas, "trifles" whose "beauty and significance" are recognized by his adopted family for the first time. Another character's loneliness is recognized only by (*) Sandy Tipton, the godfather of the title figure. This story opens with a description of gamblers who paid no heed to the gunfight between French Pete and Kanaka Joe and ends as a deluge threatens the life of the title character, held tightly by the dying Kentuck. This story is about the progeny of the title town's only female resident, Cherokee Sal. For 10 points, identify this story by Bret Harte.

After one character in this play's first act says "succulent," the other replies "you shouldn't say that word to a married woman." One character is calmed by another blowing into his mouth, though that same character agitates him by calling him "Simey" and keeps tearing newspapers into five equal strips. One character believes another character to be asleep, though he was taken away to see (*) "Monty" for "special treatment." That character beats a drum around a room before removing his glasses and being backed up against the wall during a game of blindman's bluff, during which he attempts to rape a woman. The other woman proclaims herself to be the "belle of the ball," an event during which Petey is absent and which was thrown together by Goldberg and McCann. For 10 points, identify this play about the boarder Stanley, who ages one year in a violent and absurd spectacle, the first-full length play by Harold Pinter.

Noted participants in this event included the liaison to Communist countries, Franz Konig, and the liberal Hans Kung. American opponents of this event rallied behind John Joseph Krol, while its leading dissenters worldwide organized as the International Group of Fathers and founded movements such as sedevacantism under leaders including Marcel Lefebvre and Hutton Gibson. Lesser-known documents produced at this event include a "decree on the means of social communication;" it also issued decrees such as Dignitatis humanae, on religious (*) freedom, and Nostra Aetate, which revoked the doctrine of collective Jewish guilt. Several "dogmatic constitutions" defining modern Catholicism also appeared at, for 10 points, what 1962 to 1965 summit convened by John XIII at the Papal home city?
Second Vatican Council [or Vatican II; prompt on Vatican Council]

This man received a namesake tribute of 37,000 pounds after he was charged of having a connection with the killings of Lord Henry Cavendish and Thomas Henry Burke. He was the target of a forgery campaign by Richard Pigott, even though he was mostly acquitted in the House of Commons after a trial. As the leader of a Land League, he was thrown into the Kilmainham Jail for opposing a Coercion Act. His demise came after the Nonconformist movement of his political party, after seeing a letter written to John Rowley, voted him out of a position of leadership after he was married to (*) Kitty O'Shea. A co-founder of the Irish Nationalist League, he is remembered for working with Gladstone to execute home rule for Ireland. For 10 points, name this late-19th Century politician.

Polarization density is equal to this multiplied by vacuum permittivity and electric susceptibility. The Debye length is the distance that mobile charge carriers can shield from these. The index of refraction can change due to one of these in the Kerr effect. In Faraday's law of induction, the curl of this vector is taken, while in Gauss's law the divergence of this is equal to (*) charge density divided by vacuum permittivity. This has a value of 0 outside of a capacitor and is defined as equal to the force that a test charge would feel at a given location in space. This is equal to k times charge divided by distance squared in Coulomb's law. For 10 points, name this vector that has units of newtons per coulomb.

One character in this novel possesses a collection of pornographic torture scenes and gets deported from France. Two characters living on opposite sides of a street build a bridge of boards to connect their apartment windows, though one of them builds traps with water basins and yarn to warn himself of the other's approach. Gekrepten is left behind by three friends who work at an asylum in this book, in which a car accident hospitalizes the widely-read author Morelli. Suspicions that Rocomadour's mother is involved with (*) Osip Gregorovious lead a Serpent's Club member to abandon La Maga in this work, which contains "expendable chapters" as well as a Table of Instructions at its opening. For 10 points, identify this novel which can be read by jumping through its chapters in a specified order, the magnum opus of Julio Cortazar.

His first great success was his reconstruction and completion of Weber's comic opera The Three Pintos. He adapted the story of a minstrel fashioning a flute from the bone of a murdered boy for his cantata Song of Lamentation. His third symphony includes a setting of Nietzsche's "Midnight Song" and is the longest in the standard repertory. The love letters he wrote during his disastrous affair with (*) Johanna Richter inspired his cycle Songs of a Wayfarer. Throughout much of his life he wrote songs based on the folk poems in "The Youth's Magic Horn," and he set works of Li Po and included Chinese motifs in his "The Song of the Earth." For 10 points, name this Austrian composer of "Resurrection" and "Titan" symphonies.

One text related to this religion references the actions of the priest Lohan, who received the priest Kih-ho and had earlier endured the actions of a ruler who was hostile to it. That text contains an ode that proclaims that "The sovereign has the power to act" while the ministers only have the power to record. It frequently mentions "Illustrious churches" and opens by urging the reader to "Behold the unchangingly true and invisible." Also referencing how the missionary Alopen spread this doctrine to the Taizong Emperor, that text is this doctrine's namesake (*) stele. Cyril of Alexandria wrote heavily against this heresy that argued against the use of the title "Theotokos" to refer to the Virgin Mary and was condemned at the First Council of Ephesus. For 10 points, name this early Christian heresy.
Nestorianism [prompt on "Christianity;" accept Nestorian Stele before mentioned by name in the question]

One of this author's novellas features a jester called The Liar and an Egyptian ruler named Great House. Another of his novels focuses on the priestess Arieka, who becomes the Oracle at Delphi; that work was left unfinished at his death. In addition to The Scorpion God and The Double Tongue, he also wrote about Matty, a survivor of the London bombings, and the dean Jocelin, who attempts to build the titular structure on a cathedral. This author of Darkness Visible (*) and The Spire included themes of survival and the search for order in many of his works, such as The Inheritors and a novel in which Jack steals Piggy's glasses and Ralph take care of the conch shell. For 10 points, name this British author who wrote Lord of the Flies.

It's not salicylic acid, but the turnover rate of this compound can be measured using Trinder's Reagent. It is hydrogenated in part of the Reichstein process, which eventually produces Vitamin C. The quantity of this compound present in hemoglobin is measured via the A1C test. One pathway involved in synthesizing this molecule relies on (*) PEPCK and pyruvate carboxylase, while in a different pathway it is produced from two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate exiting the Calvin Cycle. The amount of of this molecule present in the bloodstream is increased by a hormone produced in the alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans, and is decreased by insulin. For 10 points, name this monomeric sugar which in the beginning of cellular respiration is cleaved into two molecules of pyruvate.

One character in this play tells the fable of "The Snake and the Fox" in response to another character's stories about the calf that swallowed ground glass and the cock that wanted to play a dog. This play was inspired by the startling truisms its author discovered while trying to learn English. Two characters in this work kiss after realizing that they live in the same house, sleep in the same bed, and both have a (*) two year old daughter named Alice with one red and one left eye, although the maid Mary informs them that these are different daughters after all. The central couple of this play has a conversation about a family composed entirely of Bobby Watsons before entertaining the Martins and the Fire Chief. For 10 points, name this absurdist play about the Smiths by Eugene Ionesco.

This novel's frame narrative consists of a friend of the narrator asking for a government position on his behalf. The protagonist of this work is told of the provincial Heurtevent family by Alcide, a boy he catches poaching on his Norman estate called La Moriniere, which is run by the caretaker Bocage. In this novel, the narrator's wife has a miscarriage while he is away talking with the nonconformist (*) Menalque. The protagonist of this novel catches Moktir stealing scissors from him before quietly watching his wife die of tuberculosis at its conclusion. After marrying Marceline to appease his dying father, the narrator Michel exacerbates her condition by travelling all over Europe and North-Africa in search of young boys. For 10 points, name this novel by Andre Gide.

The village of Portobello merged with this city in 1896 and a dog in this city allegedly stayed at his owner's grave for 14 years, which earned him a large statue and the sorbequiet Greyfriars Bobby after the church where the cemetary was located. The Braid hills are in this city's southeast while the Pentland Hills are located to the North and the underground catacombs are known as this city's "vaults." The Princes Street Gardens stretch through the middle of this city across "The Mound," which holds this city's National Gallery, and Samson's Ribs are an unusual formation in the Salisburg Crags area of (*) Holyrood Park, which also contains Arthur's Seat. The Water of Leith is the main river in this city which drains to the River Forth and the Firth of Forth. For 10 points, identify this city whose main castle is located at the end of the Royal Mile next to the remnants of Loch Nor, the second largest city and capital of Scotland.

One of this man's last paintings was a portrait of Cupid removing Venus's clothing. He painted John the Baptist as a child dramatically raising his hand, along with a portrait of the Infant Hercules Strangling Serpents. He included a number of dogs in large paintings, such as that of the Marlborough family, and portrayed a stately blue-clad tragedy losing a contest with a mischievous looking comedy over Shakespearean actor David (*) Garrick. He painted portraits of Diana Sackville and his possible mistress, the courtesan Kitty Fisher, in addition to a rather effeminate looking Banastre Tarleton. One of his best-known paintings shows Colonel Acland and Lord Sydney hunting with bows, and another contains figures of pity and terror in the background as well as the artist' signature on the hem of the main subject's dress. For 10 points, identify this artist of The Archers as well as Sarah Siddons as the Tragic Muse, a pre-eminent 18th century British portraitist.

One of this artist's portraits shows Margaret Kemble Gage seated and wearing a pink dress with a black and gold belt. He depicted a literary character holding his shield and facing away from the viewer while faith, clad in a white gown, holds a chalice in which sits a serpent. In another painting, he depicted many red robed members of the House of Lords. This artist of The Red Cross Knight and The Death of the Earl of Chatham painted his brother seated, wearing a colorful pink collar while the title (*) animal sits on the table on which his arm is resting in Boy With a Squirrel. He painted a figure holding a silver teapot in his portrait of Paul Revere. For 10 points, name this artist who depicted a marine rescue in Havana Harbor in Watson and the Shark.

In one work by this author, a disgruntled priest posts a sign claiming that a dragon will emerge from a lake on the 3rd of March, drawing a large crowd of people who think they witness that event. The narrator of an autobiographical story by this man has an aversion to the color yellow, constantly encounters raincoats, and reads a section from The Brothers Karamazov in his copy of Crime and Punishment. That story concerns an author who hallucinates about (*) gears. In another of his stories, a recently fired servant steals clothes from an old woman after watching her gather hairs from a corpse under the title gate. This author of "The Dragon" and "Cogwheels" wrote of seven witnesses giving varying accounts of a murder of a samurai. For 10 points, name this Japanese author of "In a Grove" and "Rashomon."

This author reconsidered classic works of ethnography from a postmodernist standpoint in Works and Lives: The Anthropologist as Author. He described a syncretic village religion, the orthodox practices of Muslim merchants, and the Hinduism of government officials in The Religion of Java, while one of his essays is subtitled (*) "Religious Development in Morocco and Indonesia." In addition to "Islam Observed," this anthropologist argued against provincialism in the lecture "Anti-Anti-Relativism," and also described "webs of significance in which individuals are caught." For 10 points, identify this anthropologist who coined the term "thick description," which he employed in an essay from Interpretation of Cultures, entitled "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight."

Trout and Rankine performed a version of this experiment using a Wheatstone bridge to measure changes in resistance in a rotated circuit. This experiment was also modified by Kennedy and Thorndike, to test the length contraction hypothesis proposed by Lorentz and Fitzgerald. The original experimenters used a sodium lamp to produce a continuous beam of monochromatic light which was shot at a (*) beam splitter consisting of a half-silvered mirror. The entire apparatus of this experiment was able to be rotated relative to a hypothetical stationary reference medium, as it was constructed on a stone slab floating atop a pool of mercury. For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment with a null result which used an interferometer to disprove the concept of a luminiferous ether.

This man expressed his wonder at how people do not value what he believes to be the most precious commodity of all, time, in an essay that asked "Why do we complain of nature?" before extolling the vices of many of his contemporaries. He also wrote works addressed to Marcia, a woman who had lost her son, and to his mother Helviam Metrem explaining his exile to Corsica. This author of "On the Shortness of Life" and several (*) Consolations also wrote a play in which the title character, after being killed by Clotho, makes a case for his own deification, though he is eventually refused and escorted to the underworld. This author of The Pumpkinification of Claudius committed suicide following the Pisonian Conspiracy though he had earlier served as a tutor for the emperor Nero. For 10 points, name this noted Roman stoic philosopher.

Athena reassured this figure by sending her a vision of her sister Iphthime in a dream. She tells a stranger that dreams can come through a horn gate or an ivory gate after asking him to interpret her dream in which an eagle attacks twenty geese. Her bed was built around a giant olive tree, and her husband married her after giving her uncle (*) Tyndareus the idea of extracting an oath from the suitors of Helen or winning her in a footrace held by Icarius. Every night, she unravels a shroud that she weaves for her father in law Laertes. She withstood the advances of Eurymachus, Antinous, and a host of other pillaging suitors with the help of her son Telemachus. For 10 points, name this wife of Odysseus.

This poet recounts how he "oft spent / Narrow nightwatch nigh the ship's head / While she tossed close to the cliffs" in a poem that concludes by proclaiming that "their buried bodies / Be an unlikely treasure hoard." He called genius a "deathless adornment" in a poem whose speaker walks in the "Shades of Callimachus." This author of "The Seafarer" and "Homage to Sextus Propertius" described a figure whose "true Penelope was Flaubert" and who was "Bent resolutely on wringing lilies from the acorn" in his attempt to "resuscitate the dead art / Of poetry." In addition to (*) "Hugh Selwyn Mauberley," he described "The apparition... of these faces... in the crowd" in his poem "In a Station of the Metro." For 10 points, name this poet who included Adams and Pisan sections in his long collection, The Cantos.

This composer was discouraged by Eduard Hanslick's review of his violin concerto, a piece whose premiere was performed by an orchestra playing from poorly copied sheet music that was filled with mistakes. Another work by this composer for violin and orchestra premiered by Adolph Brodsky is his single-movement Serenade Melancolique. His first symphony includes a movement called "Land of Desolation, Land of Mists" and is named "Winter Daydreams," and he wrote a (*) Manfred Symphony in addition to his six numbered ones. His stage works include one with both a "Grandfather's Dance" and "Dance of the Mirlitons," two movements about a Christmas tree, and a "Dance of the Sugar-Plum Fairy." For 10 points, name this composer who wrote The Nutcracker and incorporated cannons into his 1812 Overture.

This character longed for a honeymoon in Switzerland, and she throws her dried up bridal bouquet into a fire in a fit of rage. A man professes to be in love with her during an agricultural fair in which a prize is awarded to a woman who has lived on the same farm for fifty-four years. She uses the pretext of piano lessons to secretly see another man, though their affair turns stale when she demands increasingly extravagant activities. Her finances are proved to be in ruin when (*) Monsieur Lheureux demands payment on the loans he has given her, and when she cannot pay he threatens to confiscate her and her husband's property. Because of this, she convinces Justin, the assistant of the pharmacist Homais, to give her a fatal dose of arsenic. For 10 points, name this wife of a doctor named Charles, the title character of a Gustave Flaubert novel.

One thinker from this country published a rebuttal of Mandeville's fable of the bees and attacked Hobbes in his essay Thoughts of Laughter after establishing an influential ethical philosophy in An Inquiry Concerning Moral Good and Evil. Another thinker from this country advocated "direct realism" in attacking the idealism of Berkeley and championed the "vulgar" or the "sensus communis." Another philosopher from this country proposed that each person is made up of a "bundle" of attributes and argued that although it is necessary in everyday life, a justification of (*) induction is impossible. That philosopher's criticism of those who offer prescriptive instead of descriptive theories is called the "is-ought" problem and found in his A Treatise of Human Nature. For 10 points, name this home of Frances Hutcheson, Thomas Reid, and David Hume.

This particle results from the gauge symmetry of the complex numbers. In Doppler cooling, this particle is shot from two directions at atoms. The Stark-Einstein law states that one molecule reacts with exactly one of these. In the Mossbauer effect, these bosons cause no recoil in solids. This spinless particle is the force carrier for the (*) electromagnetic force and the annihilation of an electron and positron results in two of these. This massless particle has momentum equal to h-bar times the wave vector and can generate current when they hit certain metals in an effect first found by Hertz. For 10 points, name this particle representing quanta of light.

This character responds by saying "Non, je ne partirai pas," or "No, I will not go," after he is told to leave in Act III, while in Act I he engages with the orphan Micaela in the duet "Parle-moi de ma mere," or "Tell me about my mother." After spending a month in prison for letting a prisoner escape, he arrives at Lillas Pastia's tavern, where his superior Zuniga (*) is captured and where he is persuaded to join the smugglers Le Dancaire and Le Remendado; this is also where he sings the aria "La fleur que tu m'avais jetee," or "The flower that you threw at me," which declares his love for a woman that sings the line "Love is a rebellious bird." This character is almost killed when he engages in a fight with the bullfighter Escamillio and in the final act, he stabs his love, a cigarette factory worker who had earlier sung the famous Habanera. For 10 points, name this opera character, a soldier who falls in love with the titular gypsy in Georges Bizet's Carmen.

This city's mayor Freeland Kendrick appointed Smedley Butler Director of Public Safety to combat its lawlessness during Prohibition. Rumors about its police beating a pregnant black woman to death sparked its 1964 race riots. The Act of Consolidation was passed in this city in 1854, ten years after rumors of Catholics removing bibles from schools led to its Nativist Riots. Under Mayor Wilson Goode, this city's government killed eleven people by dropping a bomb from a helicopter on John Africa's (*) MOVE organization. This city suffered a major Yellow Fever epidemic in 1793, and it was occupied by William Howe during the Revolution. The Paxton Boys marched on this city, which was the second capital of the United States. For 10 points, name this site of the Continental Congresses and the Liberty Bell.

One reaction of this type reacts two esters under first acidic, then basic conditions to produce beta-ketoesters. Another reaction of this type often follows a reaction in which an enolate reacts with the alpha carbon of a carbonyl to form a beta-hydroxy ketone or aldehyde. In that secondary reaction, the original product is converted to an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound. This class of reaction is exemplified by a reaction named after (*) Dieckmann which is an intramolecular version of the one named after Claisen, and a common reaction following the aldol addition. Used to make polysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids, for 10 points, name this type of of reaction in which molecules are joined together with the loss of water or another small molecule.
condensation reactions [prompt on addition reaction, do not accept dehydration reaction, since the first sentence describes the Claisen Condensation which releases an alcohol rather than water]

This architect listed among his favorite designs a 720 foot by 720 foot exposition hall that would have held 50,000 thousand people. This designer of the unrealized Chicago Convention Hall had a lengthy collaboration with the interior decorator Lilly Reich. He placed a glass facade around the rectangular frame of a building he taught in, IIT's Crown Hall. The brightness of Alexander Calder's Flamingo contrasts with the dark glass he used for the (*) Chicago Federal Center, and other Chicago structures designed by this architect include the Lakeshore Drive apartments and the stilted Farnsworth House. He collaborated with Phillip Johnson on International Style Seagram Building in New York. For 10 points, name this German architect who adopted the motto "less is more."

Throughout the 1990s, this company was the target of lawsuits over the firing of Jean Frydman, a Jewish board member, in order to comply with Arab League boycott rules. At the time, its American operations were led by Jacques Correze, who was a former Nazi collaborator alongside this company's founder, Eugene Schueller. Ironically, Scheuller's granddaughter and heir to the largest stake in this company married a Jewish man and converted to Judaism, shortly before suing a photographer who received billions of dollars in gifts, including Picasso and Matisse originals, from another shareholder in this company.
